fetched_contents.text: Mouth Breathing and Its Impact on Atypical Swallowing: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Abstract The aim of this systematic review is the assessment of the effect of mouth breathing on the prevalence of tongue thrust. The review was performed according to the PRISMA 2020 checklist guidelines, and the protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42022339527). The inclusion criteria were the following: studies of clinical trials and cross-sectional and longitudinal descriptive studies that evaluate the appearance of tongue thrust in patients with mouth breathing; healthy subjects of any age, race or sex; and studies with a minimum sample group of five cases. The exclusion criteria were the following: studies with syndromic patients, articles from case reports, and letters to the editor and/or publisher. Searches were performed in electronic databases such as The National Library of Medicine (MEDLINE via PUBMED), the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Web of Science and Scopus, including studies published until November 2023, without a language filter. The methodological quality of the included case–control studies was assessed using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS), and the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) tool was used for descriptive cross-sectional studies and cross-sectional prevalence studies. A meta-analysis was conducted on studies that provided data on patients’ classification according to mouth breathing (yes/no) as well as atypical swallowing (yes/no) using Review Manager 5.4. From 424 records, 12 articles were selected, and 4 were eligible for meta-analysis. It was shown that there is no consensus on the diagnostic methods used for mouth breathing and tongue thrust. The pooled risk ratio of atypical swallowing was significantly higher in the patients with mouth breathing (RR: 3.70; 95% CI: 2.06 to 6.66). These studies have several limitations, such as the heterogeneity among the individual studies in relation to the diagnostic tools and criteria for the assessment of mouth breathing and atypical swallowing. Considering the results, this systematic review shows that patients with mouth breathing presented higher risk ratios for atypical swallowing. Keywords: mouth breathing, oral breathing, tongue thrust, atypical swallowing, tongue habits 1. Introduction Patients with mouth breathing are at risk of developing altered dental and facial skeletal growth [1,2], sleep disorders [3] and poor quality of life [4,5,6]. The etiological factors of this common condition could be divided into obstructive and functional factors [7,8]. Tonsillar hypertrophy, deviated nasal septum and the presence of nasal polyps are among the obstructive factors. Meanwhile, functional factors include prolonged oral habits, muscular alterations or transient edema of the nasal mucosa (allergic rhinitis) [7,8]. Nasal breathing is a key factor in the correct development of the oral cavity [9,10]. When mouth breathing occurs, the lips remain open, the contraction of the mandibular elevator muscles is reduced, the perioral muscles’ activity is triggered and a lower or anterior position of the tongue is adopted. The consequences of these changes could be the development of a long face, narrow maxilla, high-arched palate, class II or class III skeletal profiles, anterior open bite, anterior or posterior crossbite, short upper lip, everted lower lip and forward head posture, among others [1,7,10,11,12,13,14]. Mouth breathing has also been associated with tongue thrust or atypical swallowing [15,16,17]. Tongue thrust consists of the introduction and support of the tongue between the incisors during swallowing. Tongue thrust has been described as a risk factor for the appearance of malocclusions associated with the proclination of the upper anterior teeth, anterior open bite, crossbite and high and/or narrow palate [1,18,19]. The tongue plays a very important role in many oral functions, such as swallowing, chewing, phonation and breathing [15]. The appearance of alterations in the tongue can alter these functions. For all these reasons, the importance of adequate management and early diagnosis of patients with mouth breathing and tongue thrust habits is evident in order to avoid or minimize their impact on the development of the dental–facial complex. However, there is a need for an assessment of the clinical diagnostic tools used to establish these two conditions and for an estimate of the association of mouth breathing with tongue thrust or atypical swallowing. Thus, a systematic review is needed to achieve these objectives and critically appraise the available studies. The aim of this systematic review is to analyze the impact of the persistence of mouth breathing on the appearance of the tongue thrust habit in terms of prevalence, assessing the diagnostic tools and assessing the quality of the available evidence. 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Protocol The protocol of this systematic review was listed in a public registry (the PROSPERO database) under reference number CRD42022339527. The PRISMA guidelines were followed in the reporting of this manuscript [20]. The main question of this systematic review was as follows: what is the prevalence of the tongue thrust habit (comparison and outcome) in the general population (population) with a diagnosis of mouth breathing (exposition)? The search strategy was defined by the Population, Intervention, Comparison and Outcomes (PICO) question: * - P = General population without syndromes; * - I = Patients with a diagnosis of mouth breathing; * - C = Presence or not of tongue thrust; * - O = Prevalence of tongue thrust or atypical swallowing. fetched_contents.text: Orofacial Myofunctional Therapy in Tongue Thrust Habit: A Narrative Review Abstract Aim and objective The respective review article is to provide an overview of the various exercises in orofacial myofunctional therapy (OMT) as a treatment modality for tongue thrust habit. Tongue thrust is the persistence of an infantile swallow pattern during late childhood. This leads to breathing and speech difficulties, open bite, and protruded teeth. During formative years, most children successfully transition from an infantile to a mature swallowing pattern. However, a few develop a retained infantile swallow and tongue thrust habit which could be due to abnormal habit like thumb sucking or an underlying cause like enlarged adenoids. Adverse effects of these habits can be avoided by early detection and intervention in a growing child. Tongue thrust can be treated in different ways with early diagnosis, removal of underlying causes, correcting tongue posture, and breaking of habit with the use of orthodontic appliances. This review article is focused on the various OMT techniques employed for the correction of tongue thrust. There are several exercises in OMT which can help a child with tongue thrust. These can be performed at home under the supervision of the child's parents. Orofacial myofunctional therapy has provided a dramatic and positive influence on patients treated for tongue thrust. The joy of eating, speaking, and correct breathing can be regained along with confidence, self-esteem, and improved quality of life. Clinically, OMT plays a positive role by not only improving swallow but also the posture of tongue, improper muscle function, and reduces relapse of previous orthodontic treatments. How to cite this article Shah SS, Nankar MY, Bendgude VD, et al. Orofacial Myofunctional Therapy in Tongue Thrust Habit: A Narrative Review. Int J Clin Pediatr Dent 2021;14(2):298–303. Keywords: Myofunctional therapy, Tongue dysfunction, Tongue habits, Tongue rest posture Background What is Tongue Thrust? Tongue thrust is a term that describes a swallowing pattern in which an individual pushes the tongue against or between the teeth. This habit has also been called deviate swallow, deviant deglutition, reversed swallow, perverted swallow, oral myofunctional disorder, visceral swallow, infantile swallowing pattern, and abnormal swallow. Tulley defines it as 1969—the forward movement of the tongue tip between the teeth to meet the lower lip during deglutition and in sounds of speech so that the tongue becomes interdental.1 When to Correct Tongue Thrust? Tongue thrusting is normal in the neonate in which the tongue lies between the gum pads and the mandible is stabilized by facial muscles during a swallow. This gradually disappears with an eruption of primary dentition. Normal mature swallow shows the positioning of the tongue high on the palate behind the maxillary incisors and no lip and cheek activity during swallowing. A transitional swallowing pattern is seen in mixed dentition, when some primary teeth are lost and permanent are yet to erupt or are erupting. This type of swallow is self-correcting. In cases of open bite mostly created by habits like thumb sucking, the tongue gets thrusted ahead to achieve a lip seal. This type of tongue thrust is called a “Simple Tongue Thrust”. “Complex tongue thrust” is seen in individuals with a diffuse open bite, seen most commonly in mouth breathers and in a child with a history of chronic nasorespiratory disease/allergies. “Retained Infantile Swallow” is when the infantile swallowing reflex perseveres after the eruption of permanent teeth. Existing studies characterize the mouth breathing-tongue thrust-atypical swallowing relationship as a co-occurring clinical constellation rather than a fully causal chain, with some evidence pointing to mutual influence and others emphasizing observational association. The strongest direct evidence comes from a systematic review and meta-analysis that explicitly assessed the effect of mouth breathing on the prevalence of tongue thrust and atypical swallowing. It found that patients with mouth breathing had a significantly higher pooled risk ratio for atypical swallowing (RR: 3.70; 95% CI: 2.06 to 6.66) [N1-F1]. The same review also aimed to assess the prevalence of tongue thrust in patients with mouth breathing [N2-R1], indicating a clear focus on the mouth-breathing-tongue-thrust link.

For tongue thrust, the evidence base is mixed in terms of direct causality. The review explicitly states that it is assessing whether mouth breathing increases the prevalence of tongue thrust [N2-R1], but the evidence provided does not establish a single direction of causation. Instead, the findings suggest that the relationship is best interpreted as a co-occurrence with confounding factors. The review’s discussion notes that there is no consensus on diagnostic methods for mouth breathing and tongue thrust, and that heterogeneity in study designs and criteria limits conclusions [N1-F1]. This implies that the observed associations may reflect shared underlying mechanisms, such as nasal obstruction, oral habits, or developmental constraints, rather than a simple one-way cause-effect relationship.

The evidence on atypical swallowing is stronger as a linked feature of mouth breathing. The systematic review explicitly links mouth breathing to atypical swallowing, with the meta-analysis showing a significant association [N1-F1]. A separate longitudinal study on tongue thrust and malocclusion adds developmental context, showing that tongue thrust can persist into adolescence and that the incidence may not decline through adolescence but rather increase [N2-R5]. While this study is not directly about atypical swallowing, it supports the idea that tongue-related oral motor behaviors can have long-term developmental trajectories, which is relevant to the broader mouth-breathing-swallowing relationship.

In terms of study designs and sample sizes, the systematic review included 12 articles and 4 were eligible for meta-analysis [N1-F1]. This means the evidence is based on a moderate number of studies rather than a single large cohort. The review also relied on cross-sectional and longitudinal descriptive studies, which makes the causal inference limited [N1-F1]. The longitudinal study on tongue thrust and malocclusion had a large cohort of 225 children, with follow-up over 13.5 years and examination at age 18 for a subset [N2-F2]. This provides stronger longitudinal support for the developmental trajectory of tongue thrust, but it does not directly link mouth breathing to atypical swallowing.

Overall, the studies directly link mouth breathing to tongue thrust and atypical swallowing, but the evidence base is more consistent with co-occurrence and shared developmental pathways than with a clear, unidirectional causal chain [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R5]. The most supportive study designs are systematic reviews and longitudinal cohort studies, while cross-sectional and observational studies are less able to establish directionality [N1-F1][N2-F2].

## How existing studies characterize the relationship between mouth breathing, tongue thrust, and atypical swallowing in children

The existing evidence in the branch reports consistently characterizes mouth breathing, tongue thrust, and atypical swallowing as a **co-occurring clinical constellation** rather than a fully causal chain. Across the studies, these features are often described as mutually related but not necessarily strictly cause-and-effect relationships; instead, they appear to share underlying developmental, nasal, and muscular pathways. The strongest evidence comes from a systematic review and meta-analysis, which explicitly assessed the effect of mouth breathing on tongue thrust and atypical swallowing, and found that mouth breathing was associated with a significantly higher risk of atypical swallowing [N1-F1].

### 1) Which studies directly link mouth breathing to tongue thrust or atypical swallowing?

The most direct link in the evidence is the **systematic review and meta-analysis on mouth breathing and atypical swallowing**. It states that the review was designed to assess the effect of mouth breathing on the prevalence of tongue thrust and atypical swallowing [N2-R1]. The review’s meta-analysis found a pooled risk ratio of 3.70 for atypical swallowing in patients with mouth breathing, indicating a strong association [N1-F1]. The same review also explicitly aimed to assess tongue thrust prevalence in patients with mouth breathing [N2-R1].

A separate **longitudinal study on tongue thrust and malocclusion** adds direct longitudinal evidence, showing that tongue thrust can persist into adolescence and that the incidence may not decline through adolescence but rather increase [N2-R5]. While this study is not directly about atypical swallowing, it supports the idea that tongue-related oral motor behaviors can have long-term developmental trajectories and thus is relevant to the broader mouth-breathing-swallowing relationship [N2-F2].

So the evidence base is strongest for **mouth breathing linked to atypical swallowing**, with **mouth breathing also linked to tongue thrust** in a systematic review framework, and **tongue thrust linked to developmental persistence** in a longitudinal study [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R5].

### 2) How often these three features co-occur and whether one is a cause, effect, or co-occurrence

The branch reports indicate that these three features often **co-occur**, but the evidence is best interpreted as **shared association or co-occurrence rather than a single unidirectional cause-effect relationship**.

The systematic review explicitly states that the association between mouth breathing and atypical swallowing was statistically significant, but it also notes that there is **no consensus on diagnostic methods** and that **heterogeneity in study design and criteria limits conclusions** [N1-F1]. This is important because it suggests that the observed association may reflect overlapping developmental or functional pathways, rather than one behavior directly causing another.

The longitudinal study on tongue thrust and malocclusion further supports a developmental trajectory in which **tongue thrust does not necessarily decline with age** and may even increase over time [N2-R5]. This implies that mouth breathing, tongue thrust, and atypical swallowing may co-occur across development and may reinforce each other over time, but the evidence still does not prove a strict cause-effect direction [N2-R5][N2-F2].

In other words, the studies are more consistent with a **co-occurring constellation** than with a clean causal chain, with mouth breathing likely acting as a **contributing factor** or **shared driver** rather than the only cause [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R5].

### 3) What study designs and sample sizes support the claims?

The evidence is supported by several study designs, but the most important distinction is between **systematic review/meta-analysis**, **longitudinal descriptive studies**, and **cross-sectional studies**.

- **Systematic review and meta-analysis**: the strongest evidence base for mouth breathing and atypical swallowing. It included 12 articles and 4 were eligible for meta-analysis [N1-F1]. The meta-analysis provided a pooled risk ratio, which is the most direct quantitative support for the association.
- **Longitudinal study on tongue thrust and malocclusion**: this provides stronger support for developmental trajectory than cross-sectional studies. It followed 225 children over 13.5 years and examined a subset at age 18 [N2-F2].
- **Cross-sectional and descriptive studies**: these are also included in the systematic review, but they are less able to establish directionality and causal inference [N1-F1].

In short, the **strongest claims** are supported by **systematic review/meta-analysis** and **longitudinal cohort studies**, while **cross-sectional studies** support associations only weakly and with less confidence [N1-F1][N2-F2].

---

## 2) Clinical and diagnostic characterization of tongue thrust and atypical swallowing in children

Clinically, **tongue thrust** and **atypical swallowing** are described as abnormal oral motor patterns that persist beyond the neonatal period and deviate from the normal mature swallow pattern.

### Clinical definitions and distinguishing features

- **Tongue thrust** is defined in the evidence as a **forward position of the tongue during rest and a thrust against or between the teeth during swallowing and speech** [N3-F3][N3-R5].
- A similar clinical source describes it as a condition when children continue to push the tongue against their teeth or position the tongue forward between their teeth [N3-R4].
- The normal mature swallow is described as positioning the tongue **high on the palate behind the maxillary incisors** with **no lip or cheek activity during swallowing** [N3-F3].
- In contrast, **atypical swallowing** is characterized by deviations from this mature pattern and may affect **speech, breathing, and oral structure** [N4-R2].
- Clinicians also note that **tongue thrust may impact articulation**, and that **tongue thrusting may impact swallowing and articulation** [N4-R3].

### How clinicians classify these behaviors

Clinicians use a variety of assessments:
- **Oral structure examination**
- **Observation during eating and drinking**
- **Articulation assessment**
- **Swallowing assessments**
- **Oral motor evaluations**
- **Speech analysis** [N4-R4][N4-R5]

The evidence also indicates that SLPs use a combination of swallowing assessments, oral motor evaluations, and speech analysis to evaluate tongue thrust and related swallowing behaviors [N4-R5].

### Age-related differences and developmental trajectories

The evidence shows clear age-related differences and developmental trajectories:
- Most children transition from an **infantile to a mature swallowing pattern** during formative years, but a few develop a **retained infantile swallow and tongue thrust habit** [N3-F3].
- The longitudinal study on tongue thrust and malocclusion reports that the incidence of tongue thrust may not decline through adolescence and may increase [N2-R5].
- A separate source notes that chronic mouth breathing varies and that oral habits can shape the face and jaw over time [N6-R4].
- Another source emphasizes that during the **2- to 7-year period**, mouth, face, and head growth continue and are shaped by breathing, eating, drinking, and speaking [N6-R5].

So clinicians should interpret these behaviors as **developmentally variable**, with the potential for persistence into adolescence and the need to consider **age-specific developmental stages** in classification [N3-F3][N2-R5][N6-R5].

---

## 3) Methodological and measurement issues affecting study conclusions

The branch reports make clear that the evidence is constrained by several methodological and measurement issues.

### Assessment tools and their reliability and validity in children

- The systematic review explicitly states there is **no consensus on diagnostic methods** for mouth breathing and tongue thrust, and that **heterogeneity in diagnostic tools and criteria** limits conclusions [N1-F1].
- It also notes that methodological quality was assessed using the **Newcastle–Ottawa Scale** for case-control studies and the **Joanna Briggs Institute tool** for descriptive cross-sectional studies [N1-F1].
- However, the evidence provided does not establish strong reliability or validity data for the specific tools used in children.

### Confounding factors

The evidence points to several confounding factors that make interpretation difficult:
- **Nasal obstruction** and **nasal disease** are among the etiological factors for mouth breathing [N1-F1].
- **Dental malocclusion** is also relevant, because tongue thrust can affect the alignment of teeth and arches [N4-R2].
- **Speech disorders** are relevant because tongue thrust may impact articulation and speech-language pathologists address speech clarity, chewing, and breathing patterns [N4-R3][N5-R5].
- The review also notes **prolonged oral habits, muscular alterations, and transient nasal mucosal edema** as functional contributors to mouth breathing [N1-F1].

### Limitations in observational or cross-sectional studies

The systematic review includes **cross-sectional and longitudinal descriptive studies**, and the meta-analysis is based on pooled data from these sources [N1-F1]. The review itself acknowledges that **heterogeneity in study design and criteria weakens causal inference** [N1-F1]. The longitudinal study on tongue thrust and malocclusion provides stronger evidence of developmental trajectory, but it still relies on **observational follow-up rather than a randomized intervention design** [N2-F2].

In conclusion, the main methodological issues are:
- **Heterogeneous diagnostic methods**
- **Limited reliability and validity evidence**
- **Confounding by nasal obstruction, dental malocclusion, and speech disorders**
- **Limitations of observational and cross-sectional studies** [N1-F1][N4-R4][N4-R5][N3-F3][N2-F2]

---

## 4) Clinical implications and treatment relevance for children

The evidence suggests that clinicians should treat mouth breathing, tongue thrust, and swallowing issues as part of a **multidisciplinary, early-intervention framework**.

### What interventions are discussed?

The interventions discussed include:
- **Myofunctional therapy** [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R4]
- **Orthodontic treatment** [N3-F3]
- **Speech therapy** [N5-R5][N3-F3]
- **Habit-breaking appliances** such as tongue cribs [N3-F3]

### Evidence for effectiveness

The narrative review on orofacial myofunctional therapy in tongue thrust habit states that OMT has provided a **dramatic and positive influence**, helping regain the joy of eating, speaking, and correct breathing, as well as improving quality of life [N3-F3]. It also reports that OMT can act as an **adjunct to orthodontic treatment** and help stabilize treated malocclusion [N3-F3].

The longitudinal study on tongue thrust and malocclusion supports the importance of **early detection and intervention**, because retained infantile swallow and tongue thrust habit can persist into adolescence [N2-R5]. It also emphasizes that most children transition from an infantile to a mature swallowing pattern, but some do not [N3-F3].

### How clinicians should prioritize or sequence management

The evidence supports a **multidisciplinary approach**:
- **Early identification** of retained infantile swallow or tongue thrust habit is emphasized [N3-F3].
- A combination of **habit-breaking appliances**, **correction of malocclusion**, and **myofunctional therapy** is recommended [N3-F3].
- **Speech therapy** is noted as part of the broader management strategy, particularly for articulation and swallow function [N5-R5].
- The review warns that treating only the **intermittent heavy force** of tongue thrusting may not address the underlying problem and can lead to **relapse** after removal of an appliance [N3-F3].

In practice, the priority sequence should be:
1. **Early identification** of the retained habit or underlying cause
2. **Multidisciplinary management**, including appliance use where appropriate
3. **Orthodontic correction** of malocclusion
4. **Myofunctional therapy** to retrain oral posture and swallow function
5. **Speech therapy** as an adjunct for articulation and swallow-related issues [N3-F3][N5-R5]

---

## Bottom line

Overall, existing studies characterize the relationship between **mouth breathing, tongue thrust, and atypical swallowing in children** as a **co-occurring clinical constellation** rather than a simple cause-effect chain. The strongest evidence comes from a **systematic review and meta-analysis** showing a significant association between mouth breathing and atypical swallowing, and from a **longitudinal study** showing that tongue thrust can persist into adolescence [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R5]. Clinically, tongue thrust and atypical swallowing are defined as abnormal oral motor patterns that persist beyond the neonatal period, with clinicians classifying them through **oral structure examination, swallowing assessments, oral motor evaluations, and speech analysis** [N3-F3][N4-R4][N4-R5]. Methodologically, the evidence is limited by **heterogeneous diagnostic methods, confounding factors, and the limitations of observational and cross-sectional studies** [N1-F1][N3-F3]. Clinically, the evidence supports **early intervention, multidisciplinary management, and integrated breathing, swallowing, and speech therapy** [N3-F3][N5-R1][N5-R5].

The strongest direct evidence comes from a systematic review and meta-analysis that explicitly assessed the effect of mouth breathing on the prevalence of tongue thrust and atypical swallowing. It found that patients with mouth breathing had a significantly higher pooled risk ratio for atypical swallowing (RR: 3.70; 95% CI: 2.06 to 6.66) [N1-F1]. The same review also aimed to assess the prevalence of tongue thrust in patients with mouth breathing [N2-R1], indicating a clear focus on the mouth-breathing-tongue-thrust link.

For tongue thrust, the evidence base is mixed in terms of direct causality. The review explicitly states that it is assessing whether mouth breathing increases the prevalence of tongue thrust [N2-R1], but the evidence provided does not establish a single direction of causation. Instead, the findings suggest that the relationship is best interpreted as a co-occurrence with confounding factors. The review’s discussion notes that there is no consensus on diagnostic methods for mouth breathing and tongue thrust, and that heterogeneity in study designs and criteria limits conclusions [N1-F1]. This implies that the observed associations may reflect shared underlying mechanisms, such as nasal obstruction, oral habits, or developmental constraints, rather than a simple one-way cause-effect relationship.

The evidence on atypical swallowing is stronger as a linked feature of mouth breathing. The systematic review explicitly links mouth breathing to atypical swallowing, with the meta-analysis showing a significant association [N1-F1]. A separate longitudinal study on tongue thrust and malocclusion adds developmental context, showing that tongue thrust can persist into adolescence and that the incidence may not decline through adolescence but rather increase [N2-R5]. While this study is not directly about atypical swallowing, it supports the idea that tongue-related oral motor behaviors can have long-term developmental trajectories, which is relevant to the broader mouth-breathing-swallowing relationship.

In terms of study designs and sample sizes, the systematic review included 12 articles and 4 were eligible for meta-analysis [N1-F1]. This means the evidence is based on a moderate number of studies rather than a single large cohort. The review also relied on cross-sectional and longitudinal descriptive studies, which makes the causal inference limited [N1-F1]. The longitudinal study on tongue thrust and malocclusion had a large cohort of 225 children, with follow-up over 13.5 years and examination at age 18 for a subset [N2-F2]. This provides stronger longitudinal support for the developmental trajectory of tongue thrust, but it does not directly link mouth breathing to atypical swallowing.

Overall, the studies directly link mouth breathing to tongue thrust and atypical swallowing, but the evidence base is more consistent with co-occurrence and shared developmental pathways than with a clear, unidirectional causal chain [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R5]. The most supportive study designs are systematic reviews and longitudinal cohort studies, while cross-sectional and observational studies are less able to establish directionality [N1-F1][N2-F2].

The evidence states that tongue thrust can force the teeth and arches out of alignment due to the constant pressure of the tongue and that it can affect speech and breathing [N4-R2]. Methodological and measurement issues significantly constrain conclusions about mouth breathing, tongue thrust, and swallowing. The most direct concern is the lack of consensus on diagnostic methods. The systematic review explicitly states that there is no consensus on the diagnostic methods used for mouth breathing and tongue thrust, and that heterogeneity among studies in diagnostic tools and criteria limits conclusions [N1-F1]. This means that findings may reflect measurement differences rather than a single, universal relationship.

Assessment tools are therefore a major limitation. The review notes that the methodological quality of included case-control studies was assessed using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale, while descriptive cross-sectional studies and cross-sectional prevalence studies were appraised with the Joanna Briggs Institute tool [N1-F1]. However, the evidence provided does not indicate strong reliability or validity data for the specific tools used in children. The review also emphasizes that heterogeneity in diagnostic criteria and tools limits conclusions, suggesting that many studies may not be directly comparable [N1-F1]. In the clinical context, clinicians use a range of assessments including oral structure examination, observation during eating and drinking, articulation assessment, swallowing assessments, oral motor evaluations, and speech analysis [N4-R4][N4-R5]. While these are clinically relevant, the evidence does not establish whether these tools are standardized, validated, or reliable across children.

Confounding factors are another major limitation. The systematic review notes that etiological factors of mouth breathing include obstructive and functional causes such as tonsillar hypertrophy, deviated nasal septum, nasal polyps, prolonged oral habits, muscular alterations, and transient nasal mucosal edema [N1-F1]. A separate source explicitly links tongue thrust to enlarged adenoids and chronic nasorespiratory disease or allergies [N3-F3]. These factors complicate interpretation because they may explain both mouth breathing and tongue-related swallowing patterns. The evidence also points to dental malocclusion as part of the clinical picture, since tongue thrust can affect alignment of teeth and arches [N4-R2]. Speech disorders are also relevant because the review notes that tongue thrust may impact articulation and that speech-language pathologists address speech clarity, chewing, and breathing patterns [N4-R3][N5-R5]. This means that observed associations may be driven by comorbid oral, nasal, and speech conditions rather than a single direct relationship.

Observational and cross-sectional studies are especially limited in establishing causality. The systematic review includes cross-sectional and longitudinal descriptive studies, and the meta-analysis is based on pooled data from these sources [N1-F1]. The review itself acknowledges that heterogeneity in study design and criteria weakens causal inference [N1-F1]. The longitudinal study on tongue thrust and malocclusion provides stronger evidence of developmental trajectory, but it still relies on observational follow-up rather than a randomized intervention design [N2-F2]. Because of these limitations, the evidence supports associations and developmental patterns more than definitive cause-effect claims [N1-F1][N2-F2].

Overall, the main methodological issues are heterogeneous diagnostic methods, limited reliability and validity evidence, confounding by nasal obstruction, dental malocclusion, and speech disorders, and the limitations of observational and cross-sectional studies [N1-F1][N4-R4][N4-R5][N3-F3]. The strongest evidence comes from a systematic review and meta-analysis, which explicitly assessed the effect of mouth breathing on tongue thrust and atypical swallowing, and found that mouth breathing was associated with a significantly higher risk of atypical swallowing [N1-F1].

### 1) Which studies directly link mouth breathing to tongue thrust or atypical swallowing?

The most direct link in the evidence is the **systematic review and meta-analysis on mouth breathing and atypical swallowing**. It states that the review was designed to assess the effect of mouth breathing on the prevalence of tongue thrust and atypical swallowing [N2-R1]. The review’s meta-analysis found a pooled risk ratio of 3.70 for atypical swallowing in patients with mouth breathing, indicating a strong association [N1-F1]. The same review also explicitly aimed to assess tongue thrust prevalence in patients with mouth breathing [N2-R1].

A separate **longitudinal study on tongue thrust and malocclusion** adds direct longitudinal evidence, showing that tongue thrust can persist into adolescence and that the incidence may not decline through adolescence but rather increase [N2-R5]. So the evidence base is strongest for **mouth breathing linked to atypical swallowing**, with **mouth breathing also linked to tongue thrust** in a systematic review framework, and **tongue thrust linked to developmental persistence** in a longitudinal study [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R5].

### 2) How often these three features co-occur and whether one is a cause, effect, or co-occurrence

The branch reports indicate that these three features often **co-occur**, but the evidence is best interpreted as **shared association or co-occurrence rather than a single unidirectional cause-effect relationship**.

The systematic review explicitly states that the association between mouth breathing and atypical swallowing was statistically significant, but it also notes that there is **no consensus on diagnostic methods** and that **heterogeneity in study design and criteria limits conclusions** [N1-F1]. This is important because it suggests that the observed association may reflect overlapping developmental or functional pathways, rather than one behavior directly causing another.

The longitudinal study on tongue thrust and malocclusion further supports a developmental trajectory in which **tongue thrust does not necessarily decline with age** and may even increase over time [N2-R5]. This implies that mouth breathing, tongue thrust, and atypical swallowing may co-occur across development and may reinforce each other over time, but the evidence still does not prove a strict cause-effect direction [N2-R5][N2-F2].

### 3) What study designs and sample sizes support the claims?

The evidence is supported by several study designs, but the most important distinction is between **systematic review/meta-analysis**, **longitudinal descriptive studies**, and **cross-sectional studies**.

## 2) Clinical and diagnostic characterization of tongue thrust and atypical swallowing in children

Clinically, **tongue thrust** and **atypical swallowing** are described as abnormal oral motor patterns that persist beyond the neonatal period and deviate from the normal mature swallow pattern.

### Clinical definitions and distinguishing features

- **Tongue thrust** is defined in the evidence as a **forward position of the tongue during rest and a thrust against or between the teeth during swallowing and speech** [N3-F3][N3-R5].

- In contrast, **atypical swallowing** is characterized by deviations from this mature pattern and may affect **speech, breathing, and oral structure** [N4-R2].
- Clinicians also note that **tongue thrust may impact articulation**, and that **tongue thrusting may impact swallowing and articulation** [N4-R3].

- **Observation during eating and drinking**
- **Articulation assessment**
- **Swallowing assessments**
- **Oral motor evaluations**
- **Speech analysis** [N4-R4][N4-R5]

The evidence also indicates that SLPs use a combination of swallowing assessments, oral motor evaluations, and speech analysis to evaluate tongue thrust and related swallowing behaviors [N4-R5].

The evidence shows clear age-related differences and developmental trajectories:

- The longitudinal study on tongue thrust and malocclusion reports that the incidence of tongue thrust may not decline through adolescence and may increase [N2-R5].

- Another source emphasizes that during the **2- to 7-year period**, mouth, face, and head growth continue and are shaped by breathing, eating, drinking, and speaking [N6-R5].

## 3) Methodological and measurement issues affecting study conclusions

The branch reports make clear that the evidence is constrained by several methodological and measurement issues.

### Assessment tools and their reliability and validity in children

- The systematic review explicitly states there is **no consensus on diagnostic methods** for mouth breathing and tongue thrust, and that **heterogeneity in diagnostic tools and criteria** limits conclusions [N1-F1].
- It also notes that methodological quality was assessed using the **Newcastle–Ottawa Scale** for case-control studies and the **Joanna Briggs Institute tool** for descriptive cross-sectional studies [N1-F1].

### Confounding factors

The evidence points to several confounding factors that make interpretation difficult:
- **Nasal obstruction** and **nasal disease** are among the etiological factors for mouth breathing [N1-F1].
- **Dental malocclusion** is also relevant, because tongue thrust can affect the alignment of teeth and arches [N4-R2].
- **Speech disorders** are relevant because tongue thrust may impact articulation and speech-language pathologists address speech clarity, chewing, and breathing patterns [N4-R3][N5-R5].
- The review also notes **prolonged oral habits, muscular alterations, and transient nasal mucosal edema** as functional contributors to mouth breathing [N1-F1].

The systematic review includes **cross-sectional and longitudinal descriptive studies**, and the meta-analysis is based on pooled data from these sources [N1-F1]. - **Heterogeneous diagnostic methods**
- **Limited reliability and validity evidence**
- **Confounding by nasal obstruction, dental malocclusion, and speech disorders**
- **Limitations of observational and cross-sectional studies** [N1-F1][N4-R4][N4-R5][N3-F3][N2-F2]

---

## 4) Clinical implications and treatment relevance for children

The evidence suggests that clinicians should treat mouth breathing, tongue thrust, and swallowing issues as part of a **multidisciplinary, early-intervention framework**.

### What interventions are discussed?

The interventions discussed include:
- **Myofunctional therapy** [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R4]
- **Orthodontic treatment** [N3-F3]
- **Speech therapy** [N5-R5][N3-F3]
- **Habit-breaking appliances** such as tongue cribs [N3-F3]

It also reports that OMT can act as an **adjunct to orthodontic treatment** and help stabilize treated malocclusion [N3-F3].

- **Early identification** of retained infantile swallow or tongue thrust habit is emphasized [N3-F3].

1. **Early identification** of the retained habit or underlying cause
2. **Multidisciplinary management**, including appliance use where appropriate

4. **Myofunctional therapy** to retrain oral posture and swallow function
5. **Speech therapy** as an adjunct for articulation and swallow-related issues [N3-F3][N5-R5]

Overall, existing studies characterize the relationship between **mouth breathing, tongue thrust, and atypical swallowing in children** as a **co-occurring clinical constellation** rather than a simple cause-effect chain. Clinically, tongue thrust and atypical swallowing are defined as abnormal oral motor patterns that persist beyond the neonatal period, with clinicians classifying them through **oral structure examination, swallowing assessments, oral motor evaluations, and speech analysis** [N3-F3][N4-R4][N4-R5]. The most direct link in the evidence is the **systematic review and meta-analysis on mouth breathing and atypical swallowing**. It states that the review was designed to assess the effect of mouth breathing on the prevalence of tongue thrust and atypical swallowing [N2-R1]. The review’s meta-analysis found a pooled risk ratio of 3.70 for atypical swallowing in patients with mouth breathing, indicating a strong association [N1-F1]. The same review also explicitly aimed to assess tongue thrust prevalence in patients with mouth breathing [N2-R1].

A separate **longitudinal study on tongue thrust and malocclusion** adds direct longitudinal evidence, showing that tongue thrust can persist into adolescence and that the incidence may not decline through adolescence but rather increase [N2-R5]. While this study is not directly about atypical swallowing, it supports the idea that tongue-related oral motor behaviors can have long-term developmental trajectories and thus is relevant to the broader mouth-breathing-swallowing relationship [N2-F2].

So the evidence base is strongest for **mouth breathing linked to atypical swallowing**, with **mouth breathing also linked to tongue thrust** in a systematic review framework, and **tongue thrust linked to developmental persistence** in a longitudinal study [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R5].

### 2) How often these three features co-occur and whether one is a cause, effect, or co-occurrence

The branch reports indicate that these three features often **co-occur**, but the evidence is best interpreted as **shared association or co-occurrence rather than a single unidirectional cause-effect relationship**.

The systematic review explicitly states that the association between mouth breathing and atypical swallowing was statistically significant, but it also notes that there is **no consensus on diagnostic methods** and that **heterogeneity in study design and criteria limits conclusions** [N1-F1].
